content:
I was reading over the proof mode, and couldn't really figure out why we have e and tm fields in the definition of Hyps.

inductive Hyps {prop : Q(Type u)} (bi : Q(BI $prop)) : (e : Q($prop)) → Type where
  | emp : Hyps bi iprop(emp)
  | sep {elhs erhs : Q($prop)}
    (tm : Q($prop))
    (lhs : Hyps bi elhs)
    (rhs : Hyps bi erhs)
    : Hyps bi iprop($elhs ∗ $erhs)
  | hyp {p : Q(Bool)} {ty : Q($prop)}
    (tm : Q($prop))
    (name uniq : Name)
    : Hyps bi iprop(□?$p $ty)

The only difference I see between them is how Hyps.mkHyp treats them, where tm is constructed using mkIntuitionisticIf, which decides statically whether to write □ $e or $e depending on if $p is the constant true or not, whether e is the "unevaluated" □?$p $ty.

Is this the only reason why e and tm are kept? What is the though process behind it? Why not just have p be a Bool instead of Q(Bool) if it's going to be used as such?

This design of Hyps predates my time in Iris Lean, so I am not sure about this. I think @Mario Carneiro would be the person to know this. In general, I hope that the exact encoding of Hyps does not matter so much, but that the functions provided by Hyps hide all these details.
It is indeed not a blocker, just something that got me curious while trying to understand the code
It is a good question and I am actually curious about it as well :)

It's generally better to keep around the Exprs even if they are redundant, to avoid the cost of recreating them and also to improve expression reuse. Qq also handles expressions like Q(Bool) better than auto-lifted meta-types.
IIRC tm is the input expression itself. It is only the same as the index e up to defeq
Yes, the only difference I could notice is in the leaves, with the □?$p $ty vs $ty. I guess we could document this in a comment or something ( :gear: )
right, tm is properly normalized while the type signature of hyp would lead you to believe that □?p ty occurs
it could have been two variants but we have several lemmas which can work directly on the □?p ty form
But then, why have the bool be an Expr (or Q(Bool))? I don't understand the comment on "auto-lifted meta-types".
You still need to be able to use p inside the types of later things, as in the type of the constructor itself
Qq has dependent types after all

so p : Expr isn't really an option to make it typecheck, and p : Bool requires Qq to insert a coercion to Q(Bool) and Qq is not good at reasoning about this coercion, it tends to cause breakage because it won't be equal to itself and other things like that

I guess my issue with it being a Q(Bool) is that it leads me to believe that this p could be an arbitrary Bool expression, but we later only use it as if it were a concrete Bool. But I see how, if this p is going to be used extensively, then having to do something like p.toExpr everywhere ends up being annoying
also, the Q(Bool) expression itself will appear in proof terms that manipulate the hyp
so it's not entirely meta-level

Yes there are several invariants on this (and most other) Qq data structures that cannot be expressed in the types. Sometimes we can insert things like $tm =Q $elhs ∗ $erhs but it's usually just an approximation of the true invariants sufficient for Qq to behave well
Yes, I was just wondering what those invariants where, so we could have them written down somewhere. Maybe even include them in the docstring.

I'm reconstructing them from memory and looking at the type, but I think they are at least:

  • The variable p is a bool literal
  • the variable tm is a cached value constructed recursively:
    • tm .emp = iprop(emp)
    • tm (.sep lhs rhs) = iprop($(tm lhs) ∗ $(tm rhs))
    • tm (.hyp q(false) ty) = ty
    • tm (.hyp q(true) ty) = iprop(□ $ty)
  • I think there are no balance invariants, but perhaps emp is not allowed to appear as an argument to sep
adding some kind of AVL balance seems like a possible future addition if it needs performance optimization
Another question that came up is, why use a tree structure? Why not just use a hashmap on the uniq names of hypotheses?
I think the point I just mentioned should answer that
Reasons I could think of where regarding sharing of nodes, to prevent having too much duplicated data, but no idea why
The kernel doesn't handle hashmaps well
all of the actual manipulations have to happen inside proofs, so we need a structure reflecting the term itself
we could have a hashmap alongside which allows fast meta-lookups but usually we want to perform a (proof traced) manipulation afterward

under the current design we also have to rediscover the structure between tactics, since we can't store global state and have to shove everything into the goal type. This is unfortunate, lean 3 had a facility for making custom tactic state extensions. But that means that there is little advantage to building a hashmap since it would have to be rebuilt on every line
I guess this means having shared state between tactics would imply creating our own kind of by elaborator? I wonder how that would play with things like the InfoView
Exactly, in lean 3 there was begin[foo] ... end which would allow you to define a Foo.Tactic type and it would usually be a StateT MyState TacticM
conv used to be done using this mechanism, now it's just reusing Tactic
I think grind => might be doing something like this as well now, but I assume it's not user-extensible

Just leaving a message here so I don't forget it later, but it may be interesting to consider making tm a @[computed_field] of our Hyps definition, like Lean.Expr does. That way we could, potentially, remove the need to use mkEmp, mkSep and mkHyp, and just use the Hyps constructors directly
